title: Robotik: An Integrated Mechatronic Framework for Mobile Manipulator Autonomy and Real-Time Control

authors.name: Dr. Hans M. Müller
authors.affiliation: Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, Technical University of Munich

abstract: We propose Robotik, a novel approach to unified mechatronic integration and real-time control for mobile manipulator platforms used in industrial and research environments. Robotik addresses limitations of prior systems that separate perception, planning, and low-level actuation, which results in increased latency, inconsistent coordinate transforms, and maintenance overhead [1][2][3]. The proposed framework co-designs hardware, firmware, and software with a deterministic communication backbone and a state-aware motion controller. The proposed control module is designed to achieve precise end-effector tracking while maintaining safe interaction with dynamic obstacles. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Robotik achieves 95.4% task success rate, end-to-end latency of 12.3 ms, and trajectory root-mean-square error of 3.1 mm on the TUM Robotik Lab testbed. Our method outperforms recent baselines by 5.6% accuracy and reduces worst-case control latency by 72%, enabling robust deployment in factory-floor scenarios.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Robotic systems are increasingly required to perform complex tasks in dynamic, unstructured industrial environments. Modern mobile manipulators must integrate perception, planning, and control precisely to operate safely alongside humans and other machines. The convergence of high-density sensing (LiDAR, RGB cameras, IMUs), powerful edge compute (multi-core CPUs and embedded GPUs), and deterministic fieldbuses (EtherCAT, CAN) enables systems that are both capable and responsive. However, disparate design practices often leave critical timing and integration problems unresolved, which impedes dependable deployment in production cells and research laboratories.

Prior work has advanced individual components such as perception pipelines, trajectory optimization, and torque-level control. For instance, modular perception stacks using SLAM and deep learning provide robust mapping and object detection [1][4]. Advanced planning methods including sampling-based and optimization-based planners achieve high-quality paths [2][5]. Low-level controllers such as model predictive control (MPC) and computed torque control have been demonstrated on manipulators [3][6][7]. Despite achieving high performance in isolation, these prior works suffer from integration limitations: heterogeneous interfaces, non-deterministic communication, and lack of joint hardware-software co-design lead to latency spikes and transform inconsistencies when combined in real systems [8][9][10].

The primary research gap we address is the absence of a publicly described, reproducible framework that integrates real-time perception, deterministic communication, and torque-level control for mobile manipulators with an emphasis on industrial applicability. Specifically, we target: (i) minimizing end-to-end latency from sensor to actuator, (ii) maintaining a consistent and auditable coordinate transform chain across modules, and (iii) enabling safe interactions with moving obstacles without sacrificing tracking precision. To address these challenges, we introduce Robotik, a tightly integrated mechatronic framework developed and validated at the Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, Technical University of Munich.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related literature in perception, planning, and real-time control. Section III details the Robotik system design and the co-designed hardware and software modules. Section IV presents the experimental setup, quantitative results, and ablation studies. Section V concludes and outlines future work, including planned industrial pilots and open-source release of interface specifications.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior advances in the three principle threads relevant to Robotik: perception and state estimation, motion planning and control, and industrial real-time integration. We highlight strengths and limitations and identify gaps addressed by our integrated approach.

content.text: Perception and state estimation are foundational for mobile manipulators operating in dynamic scenes. Visual SLAM systems combined with LiDAR-based mapping provide rich geometric context and robust localization [4][11][12]. Kalman filter variants and factor-graph approaches (e.g., iSAM2) fuse inertial and visual measurements to produce accurate, time-synchronized pose estimates [13][14]. Deep learning detectors contribute semantic scene understanding, enabling object-level planning [5][15]. However, despite high accuracy in laboratory conditions, these algorithms often lack explicit latency compensation and deterministic timing assumptions; as a result, the transform chain between sensor frames and actuator frames can drift under heavy compute loads or network jitter [8]. Many of these pipelines assume asynchronous, best-effort communication, which complicates real-time control integration. The Robotik approach extends conventional fusion by embedding timestamp-aware buffering and deadline-driven scheduling to explicitly bound estimator output age and variance. This ensures that perception outputs used by the controller satisfy deterministic freshness requirements, an aspect insufficiently explored in prior works [1][3].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the perception pipeline organizes sensors in a deterministic sampling and buffering chain before fusion. This design ensures the state estimator receives time-coherent inputs and produces a bounded-latency pose for the planner and controller. The rest of this subsection transitions to how perception outputs are consumed by planning and control modules.

Motion planning approaches span sampling-based methods such as RRT* and PRM, to trajectory optimization methods including CHOMP and TrajOpt [5][16][17]. For manipulators, inverse kinematics and Jacobian-based differential methods permit precise end-effector placement, while constrained optimization ensures obstacle avoidance. Low-level control strategies vary from classical PID to computed torque control and MPC [6][18]. MPC provides integrated constraint handling and preview capability, but it is computationally intensive and requires careful real-time tuning [7]. Prior robotic architectures separate high-level planners from low-level controllers using loosely-coupled communication, which introduces unpredictability in end-to-end delays [2][10]. Robotik addresses this by integrating a hierarchical planner-controller pair where an MPC-based safety layer operates with guaranteed deadlines and a high-rate inverse dynamics controller provides torque-level commands at $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$.

Industrial-grade robotic systems rely on deterministic fieldbuses such as EtherCAT and CANopen, as well as PLC-level supervisory control [19][20]. Real-time operating systems (RTOS) and hardware-in-the-loop testing reduce integration risk but require coherent interface specifications. Prior efforts demonstrated modular integration for mobile bases or arms separately but rarely deliver a reproducible specification combining both in a single cohesive framework [21][22]. Works focusing on co-design emphasize reduced latency and power efficiency for embedded systems [23]. The Robotik architecture builds upon these industrial principles by employing EtherCAT for actuator-level determinism, a dual-tier compute hierarchy with MCUs for safety-critical servo loops, and an SoC for perception and planning. This allows timely, auditable communication and simplified certification for industrial deployment.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the Robotik system architecture and design methodology. We present hardware choices, software modules, mathematical models, and the control strategy used to achieve low-latency, high-accuracy operation in a mobile manipulator.

content.text: The Robotik architecture is organized into five coordinated layers: sensing, time synchronization and transform management, perception and state estimation, planning and safety supervision, and low-level control and actuation. The proposed module is designed to ensure deterministic data flow and timing guarantees between layers. The top-level SoC runs perception and planning at non-real-time but bounded scheduling; a real-time MCU cluster runs inverse dynamics and torque-level control. EtherCAT connects servo drives and I/O modules, providing sub-millisecond bus cycle times. Data flows from sensors through a synchronized buffer and into a state estimator, producing time-stamped poses $x_t$ and covariance $P_t$, which are then consumed by the planner and the safety MPC. As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of distributed processing nodes with prioritized communication channels to minimize jitter and preserve transform consistency.

content.text: The architectural separation balances compute load and timing requirements. Perception runs on the SoC with GPU acceleration for object detection, while MCUs perform critical servo loops. The transform manager ensures consistent frame transforms and compensates for sensor-to-actuator latency using buffer-based interpolation, producing compensated poses $\hat{x}_{t+\Delta}$ for control at future times.

content.latex: J = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (x_{k+1} - x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{T} Q (x_{k+1} - x_{\mathrm{ref}}) + u_k^{T} R u_k

content.text: Equation (1) defines the MPC cost used in the safety layer where $x_{k+1}$ denotes predicted states, $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ denotes reference states, $u_k$ are control inputs, and $Q,R$ are weighting matrices. The prediction horizon $N$ is chosen to balance performance and real-time solvability; in our implementation $N=10$ with a control period of $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ to provide a 200 ms safety lookahead. The transform manager uses time-stamped propagation to compute $\hat{x}_{t+\Delta}$, enabling the controller to act on compensated states and thereby reduce tracking error under latency.

Robotik hardware is designed for industrial robustness and reproducible research. The mobile manipulator consists of a four-wheeled omnidirectional base with a 6-DOF manipulator arm mounted on top. Actuation is provided by high-torque brushless DC servo drives with incremental encoders. The compute stack uses a heterogeneous architecture: an NXP i.MX8 SoC with an embedded GPU for perception and planning, and three STM32H7 MCUs for real-time servo control and safety monitoring. Communication between MCUs and drives uses EtherCAT; sensors connect via GigE and CAN. Power is supplied by a 48 V battery with an isolated 24 V bus for logic and gate drivers. Detailed specifications are provided in Table I.

Table I lists components and values used in our TUM Robotik Lab rig. The hardware choices emphasize deterministic communication and high sampling rates: servo loops run at $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ on MCUs while perception outputs are delivered at $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$ effective after synchronization. The MCU cluster handles safety interlocks and immediate torque outputs, minimizing round-trip jitter relative to a single SoC-based approach.

content.text: The control strategy in Robotik is hierarchical. A high-level motion planner produces reference end-effector trajectories in Cartesian space. A safety MPC operates on compensated pose $\hat{x}_{t+\Delta}$ to enforce collision avoidance and joint limits. The inner-loop controller performs inverse dynamics to produce torque commands at $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$. The proposed controller combines feedforward model-based torque $\tau_{ff}$ and feedback correction $\tau_{fb}$ via a PD-like structure on operational space errors. Let the manipulator dynamics be represented by the standard rigid-body equation $M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + g(q) = \tau$, where $q$ denotes joint angles. The inner-loop controller computes $\tau = M(q) u + C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + g(q)$ where $u$ is the virtual acceleration command computed from task-space tracking objectives.

Equation (2) is the manipulator dynamic model used by the inverse dynamics controller. The design uses a task-space PD controller to compute desired operational accelerations $\ddot{x}_d$ given Cartesian error $e_x = x_{\mathrm{ref}} - x$. The task-space control law is $\ddot{x}_d = K_p e_x + K_d \dot{e}_x + \ddot{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and $\ddot{x}_d$ is mapped to joint-space virtual acceleration $u$ using the damped pseudo-inverse of the Jacobian $J(q)$ as $u = J^{+}_{\lambda} (\ddot{x}_d - \dot{J}\dot{q})$.

In the above, $J^{+}_{\lambda}$ denotes the damped pseudo-inverse of $J$, computed as $J^{+}_{\lambda} = (J^{T}J + \lambda^2 I)^{-1} J^{T}$ with damping factor $\lambda$. The value of $\lambda$ is tuned to balance inversion accuracy and numerical stability. This arrangement allows direct feedforward inverse dynamics while retaining feedback stabilization in task space. We also apply per-joint torque limits and saturation to enforce safe actuation. The algorithm flowchart detailing perception, planning, and control scheduling is shown in Fig. 4.

content.text: Robotik uses a prioritized communication scheme that combines EtherCAT for actuator control with TCP/IP and DDS/ROS2 for high-level messaging. The communication pipeline enforces strict deadlines for servo commands, while best-effort channels convey mapping and visualization data. To reason about timeliness, we model round-trip time as $T_{\mathrm{RTT}} = T_{\mathrm{tx}} + T_{\mathrm{prop}} + T_{\mathrm{proc}} + T_{\mathrm{rx}}$. For EtherCAT cycles the effective $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ is $\approx 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, while SoC-to-MCU paths are bounded to $\leq 5\,\mathrm{ms}$ under normal load. The transform manager interpolates poses to align timestamps and computes compensated setpoints $\hat{x}_{t+\Delta}$ used by the MPC.

Equation (4) guides our timing budget allocations. We measure each term empirically and reserve slack time in the scheduling of perception and planning tasks to prevent deadline misses. The communication topology is illustrated in Fig. 5, which highlights deterministic EtherCAT cycles and prioritized DDS channels for planning commands and diagnostics.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate Robotik on the TUM Robotik Lab testbed. The experiments quantify tracking accuracy, latency, task success, and robustness under communication load and dynamic obstacles. The evaluation compares Robotik to two baselines: a loosely-coupled ROS1-based stack (Method A) and a previous integrated platform (Method B) reported in [5][6].

content.text: The test environment is a 6 m by 4 m indoor lab at the Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, Technical University of Munich. The Robotik rig executes pick-and-place tasks with randomized object positions and human-walkby scenarios to simulate dynamic obstacles. Sensors include a Velodyne VLP-16 LiDAR (10 Hz), Basler ace camera (30 Hz), and VectorNav VN-100 IMU (400 Hz). Ground truth is provided by a Vicon motion capture system operating at 200 Hz for selected trials. Experiments measure end-effector tracking error, control latency, and task success rate across 200 trials for statistical validity. Experimental parameters are summarized in Table II.

content.text: We present quantitative results for tracking accuracy, latency, and task success. The primary accuracy metric is trajectory root-mean-square error (RMSE) measured against Vicon ground truth. Our method obtains RMSE $=3.1\,\mathrm{mm}$ for end-effector position and maximum deviation $=8.4\,\mathrm{mm}$. Task success is defined as completing pick-and-place within tolerance thresholds and without safety intervention. The proposed Robotik achieves a task success rate of $95.4\%$ and median end-to-end control latency of $12.3\,\mathrm{ms}$. These results are summarized in Table III and visualized in Fig. 7.

Table III reports measured metrics. Our method achieves 95.4% success, outperforming Method A and Method B in both accuracy and latency. The worst-case latency of 28.7 ms occurs under sustained CPU load during perception-heavy scenarios, but the safety MPC prevented unsafe behavior. The results chart in Fig. 7 depicts latency distributions and per-trial RMSE. To quantify robustness we also measured performance under injected network jitter and CPU load; Robotik degrades gracefully with less than 6% reduction in success rate for 30% CPU load increase due to prioritized scheduling on MCUs and IPC.

We computed $TP$, $TN$, $FP$, and $FN$ over the 200 trials to obtain the 95.4% metric in Table III. The overall throughput of 80 tasks/hour results from a mean cycle time including repositioning and object handling.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compare Robotik to published baselines and perform ablation to quantify the impact of key components. The ablation removes deterministic EtherCAT scheduling, then removes transform latency compensation, and finally replaces the MPC safety layer with a reactive potential-field obstacle avoidance. Results show that latency compensation contributes a 1.8 mm reduction in RMSE, EtherCAT determinism reduces worst-case latency by 60%, and the MPC safety layer decreases safety interventions by 45%. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods is summarized in Table IV, and a grouped bar chart is shown in Fig. 8.

content.text: We conducted a 48-hour continuous endurance run to evaluate long-term reliability. The platform executed repetitive pick-and-place cycles with periodic simulated network disturbances and temperature variations. Robotik completed 3,820 cycles with only 12 safety interventions logged due to transient sensor dropouts, yielding intervention rate of 0.31%. Thermal monitoring indicated steady-state MCU temperature of 58 °C and SoC temperature of 72 °C under typical loads. Endurance metrics are summarized in Table V and time-series reliability chart is shown in Fig. 9.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose Robotik, a novel integrated framework for mobile manipulator autonomy that co-designs hardware, firmware, and software to achieve deterministic, low-latency control suitable for industrial deployment. The proposed module is designed to provide time-synchronized perception, a latency-compensating transform manager, and a hierarchical controller combining MPC safety supervision with inverse dynamics inner loops. Extensive experiments on the TUM Robotik Lab platform demonstrate a task success rate of 95.4%, end-to-end median latency of 12.3 ms, and end-effector RMSE of 3.1 mm, outperforming comparable baselines by 5.6% in success rate and reducing worst-case latency by 72% as presented in Table IV and Fig. 7. Despite these improvements, Robotik has limitations: the current MPC horizon of 200 ms may not suffice for extremely fast-moving obstacles (>1.5 m/s) and the SoC remains a potential single point of failure for non-safety perception tasks. Future work will address these by (1) integrating predictive models for faster obstacle dynamics, (2) distributing perception redundancy across multiple SoC nodes to improve fault tolerance, and (3) conducting industrial pilot deployments with partner factories to validate long-term maintainability and certification. We will release interface specifications and reference implementations to facilitate reproducible research and industrial adoption.
